Because when we study opinions as opinions, what we learn is not the objective reality that exists independently of the opinion, but the human consciousness of that reality—a consciousness that may be right or wrong.
Truth, by contrast, reveals precisely this reality to consciousness.
In other words, studying opinions or ideologies tells us who expresses them. Studying truth tells us what they express.
Opinion therefore reveals human consciousness, independently of the reality outside that consciousness. Truth reveals reality, independently of the consciousness in which that reality appears.
We can therefore say that truth is reality itself insofar as it reveals itself to human consciousness and becomes accessible to knowledge.

And since human beings can obviously know only a reality that has been “revealed” in this way, it is more accurate to say that human beings seek to know the truth than to say that they seek to “know reality” or “know what is real.”

This knowledge of truth is achieved when the opinion a human being identifies with—that is, the content of his consciousness—fully coincides with truth itself: with reality as “revealed” to consciousness.
There is no doubt that this “revelation” or “disclosure” of reality takes place through human consciousness and, ultimately, through human discourse.
So when we define truth as “reality disclosing itself”—that is, as reality “revealing itself to itself”—we may seem to be introducing some “mystical” conception of reality.
But it appears mystical only because of the “idealist” prejudice deeply rooted in our thinking.
We all have the firm idea that reality somehow “enters” our consciousness. What we tend to forget is that our consciousness is itself part of reality.

Suppose, for example, that we are talking about the solar system. We must remember that this conversation is not taking place outside space and time. It is taking place inside the solar system itself.
We can therefore say that, in the conversations we have about it, the solar system itself is in a sense “revealing” itself to itself.

If, for whatever reason, the temperature of the Sun suddenly rose or fell dramatically, humanity would disappear. And with humanity would disappear every theory, every opinion, and every conversation about the Sun.
These theories and discussions therefore depend in some way on the Sun itself. In a certain sense, they are consequences of its activity just as much as the evaporation of seas and oceans is.
If that is so, then we have to say that, through humanity and through human discourse, the solar system itself in a sense “reveals” itself to itself.
It becomes an astronomical “truth” when the meaning of the discourse produced within it coincides with what the solar system actually is.
There is nothing “mystical” about this. On the contrary, it is a “realist,” or if one prefers “materialist,” conception of truth—one that shows truth itself to be something real.
We can now understand why the only guarantee that an opinion is true is its realization, whether through technology or through politics.

An opinion can become knowledge—that is, can coincide with truth—if and only if, through work and struggle, it itself becomes in some way a real part of the world. It thereby becomes part of the reality that “reveals” itself to itself.
From the “realist,” or “materialist,” standpoint established by Phenomenology, truth is therefore reality itself as disclosed in coherent discourse.
Knowledge is the opinion that coincides with truth: coherent discourse whose meaning has become real.
Truth and knowledge are two sides of one and the same thing.
Truth is the objective side of knowledge: the reality that is “disclosed” in the discourse constituting that knowledge.
Knowledge is the subjective side of truth: the content of human consciousness, or of opinion, that corresponds to this truth.
It follows from this definition that truth can exist only where there is a reality corresponding to the meaning of the discourse that expresses that truth.
And it follows in turn that knowledge exists only where the meaning of the corresponding opinion has been realized.

So if Phenomenology is supposed to make true philosophical knowledge possible—and if this first of all requires it to show the philosopher that such knowledge is possible—then Phenomenology must investigate the boundaries and limits of both reality and realization.

When it comes to reality itself—that is, to nature—the problem is relatively simple. We can say that nature has, in a sense, exhausted all its real possibilities from all eternity and remains eternally unchanged. In other words, the natural side of truth has existed since the “beginning of time.” What develops is only our knowledge of it: human ideas about nature gradually come closer to the truth.

This happens by putting those ideas into practice through technology. So, with regard to the natural world, the task of Phenomenology is to establish the limits of this realization. It must show that while natural reality already exists in its entirety, the process of realizing our ideas about nature is not yet complete. Human beings therefore do not yet possess, and cannot yet possess, complete knowledge of the natural world. Complete knowledge would exist when reality as it is independently of our ideas fully coincided with the practical realization of those ideas.

We can see this process of realization in the distinctive “technical world” that human beings have created within the natural world—a world made by us and for us on the basis of our knowledge of nature. And we can see that this process remains incomplete because the natural world and the technical world do not yet fully coincide: nature can still disrupt the internal order of the world we have created.

The situation is much more complicated when we turn to the human world. Here, reality itself has not yet reached its completion. Human beings have not yet, in our time, exhausted all their real possibilities. One of the central tasks of Phenomenology is therefore to show that human reality is unfinished.

In the case of humanity, or the historical world, it is not only knowledge that is incomplete. Truth itself is incomplete as well. There is not yet any fully true knowledge of humanity, and there cannot yet be. This is not merely because such knowledge is still developing, but because human beings themselves are still in the process of realizing what they can become. There is not yet a final truth about humanity because humanity itself is not yet, so to speak, fully “true.”

This difference between natural reality or truth and human reality or truth means that realizing ideas about nature is not the same as realizing ideas about human beings. Developing and changing our ideas about nature does not change nature itself. But changing the ideas human beings have about themselves is part of the very process by which they realize themselves, and partly determines that process. So, in the human world, establishing the limits of what human beings can think about themselves is in part the same thing as establishing the limits of what human beings themselves can become.

But the two are not completely identical. True knowledge cannot go beyond truth itself, and human beings can be known only to the extent that they have realized themselves. Yet they do not immediately become conscious of what they have already become. A “new” kind of human being often continues to hold old ideas about humanity—and therefore about itself.

Phenomenology must take this into account. It must draw the philosopher’s attention to the possible gap between humanity’s actual realization and the way that realization is reflected in human consciousness.
And even that is not enough. We must also distinguish between what is familiar to human beings and what they actually know or understand.

The situation is similar to our knowledge of the natural world. Someone may simply not know that the Earth travels around the Sun in an ellipse. But someone may also know this without understanding why it is so. The same is true of changes that have taken place in humanity. A change may be familiar to us, yet we may either fail to understand it altogether or understand it more or less incorrectly.

Phenomenology must therefore establish not only how far humanity has actually realized itself and how much of that realization has become familiar to human beings, but also how much of it they genuinely understand. And then, as we will see, it will repeatedly turn out that the “new” human being understands the “old” better than the old human being understood himself.

In any case, Phenomenology must show that perfect knowledge—knowledge that is absolutely true—is possible only when truth itself is complete, which means when reality has fully realized all of its possibilities. It must show that such knowledge will actually exist when human beings not only grasp reality in its entirety but know it completely. Phenomenology must therefore show the philosopher that none of these three processes has yet reached its end at the time he is writing it.

Everything we have said so far about Phenomenology follows from its purpose: to prepare the possibility of philosophical knowledge. The first essential feature of such knowledge is its self-awareness. We can now turn to its second essential feature: its concreteness.

Philosophy seeks knowledge of actual reality—of what really or “concretely” exists—not of an “abstraction” that exists only in human consciousness, that is, in the “imagination.” As we already know, only reality as a whole exists concretely, not its separate parts. What concretely exists, for example, is “this table at a particular moment in time and in a particular place within the real universe.” What does not concretely exist is an isolated table located nowhere in particular and at no particular time.

And, as we already know, the real universe includes human beings themselves and everything they actually do, whether they are actively changing the world or passively observing it. The concrete solar system, for example, includes not only its planets and their natural, material movements. It also includes the Earth and its human world—and therefore, among other things, human knowledge of the solar system, whether true or false, right down to this very sentence I am writing now.

Phenomenology must teach the philosopher to take this aspect of concreteness seriously. When speaking about reality, the philosopher must also include the consciousness to which, within which, and through which that reality “reveals itself” in coherent discourse.

There can be discourse about the world only where human beings live, and human beings can speak about the world only because they live within it. So we cannot speak about concrete reality by concentrating either on the world alone or on humanity alone. What concretely exists is a world that includes human beings—or, which amounts to the same thing, human beings who exist within a world.

Knowledge of concrete reality therefore cannot be reduced either to knowledge of the world taken by itself or to knowledge of humanity taken by itself. It must be knowledge of both together, understood through their actual interaction.

A philosopher who has passed through the school of Phenomenology will therefore differ from the ordinary person—the so-called “naive realist”—who can speak, for example, about the Sun while completely forgetting that he is speaking about it and that he is the one speaking.

The “naive” person thinks he is talking about concrete reality when in fact he is talking only about the “ob-ject” of his consciousness: something present within consciousness as referring to something outside it. It then turns out that he is not only failing to speak about concrete reality; strictly speaking, he is failing to speak about reality at all. If he is speaking about anything, it is merely his own subjective impression. A person speaking “naively” about the Sun would therefore have to describe it as a disc about the size of a plate, and so on.

But the philosopher also differs from the critical “scientist” who corrects the naive person’s mistakes. The scientist does introduce consciousness into the picture, since he distinguishes subjective illusion from objective reality. In trying to discover what reality is “really” like, he studies the way reality enters human consciousness.
But he does so only in order to eliminate everything purely subjective afterward—and, along with it, consciousness itself.

Admittedly, science, especially the theory of relativity and quantum mechanics, has recently understood that consciousness cannot simply be eliminated. Without it, nothing can be known about reality, since actual consciousness of reality modifies reality itself. Yet when science introduces the subject into its account, it reduces the subject to an extreme simplification. It is interested only in sensory perception, and even that only in a schematic form.

In the end, science takes account only of the fact that human beings must actually see reality in order to know something about it. It completely ignores the further fact that they must also think about reality and in some way speak about it—that is, express it, for example, in mathematical formulas.
Science therefore never deals with concrete reality either. It is always content with knowing abstractions that have no actual existence in space and time.

A complete “scientific” knowledge of the natural world—say, a complete physics—does not even set itself the task of explaining why this very scientific knowledge of the natural world exists within that world, together with the discourse in which the knowledge is expressed.

When the “scientist” speaks about the world, he forgets, more or less consciously, that he is speaking about it and that he is the one doing the speaking. Yet he can only speak about the world that he actually speaks about, and that world really includes both this human being and his discourse. So the scientist, precisely insofar as he remains a “scientist,” does not speak about the concrete world. He speaks about an abstraction that exists as such only within the scientist’s consciousness.

The philosopher, by contrast, seeks knowledge of concrete reality. He must therefore study a world that includes knowledge of that very world—or, which amounts to the same thing, study a consciousness that contains knowledge of the real world in which that consciousness itself actually exists.
Finally, Phenomenology must also help the philosopher avoid falling into religious—or, more precisely, theological—error.

As we will see later, when human beings speak about “gods,” they are not simply telling “fables.” Without realizing it, they are really speaking about themselves: they give their “gods” characteristics they have first discovered in themselves.
The theologian thinks he is talking about God. The phenomenologist shows that he is in fact talking about himself.

One of the central tasks of Phenomenology is therefore not only to show that true knowledge of humanity is incompatible with belief in the existence of God, but also to uncover the human meaning behind different theologies.

Phenomenology shows that human beings fall into theological error because, in their knowledge, they adopt the “naive” or “scientific” standpoint. In other words, they forget to include within their knowledge of reality that very knowledge of reality itself. As a result, they are not dealing with concrete reality but with an abstraction just as “nonexistent” as their “God.”

The “naive” person, like the “scientist,” is accustomed to projecting the contents of consciousness beyond consciousness and treating them as realities that exist independently of him. He therefore tends to do the same with contents of consciousness that actually refer to himself. He treats them as some “objective” reality that is human-like or “anthropomorphic,” yet supposedly exists outside or independently of humanity. It therefore appears to him as “divine” or “theomorphic.”

But once we try to have concrete knowledge of “God”—that is, once our knowledge of God includes the fact that it is a human being who knows God and speaks about God—it becomes clear that no such concrete reality exists or could exist, because the idea contains an internal contradiction.
It turns out that if human beings can speak, this is only because there is no God.
We can therefore say that, in teaching the philosopher to seek concrete knowledge of himself, Phenomenology also tends to teach him to be an atheist.

All of this will become clearer and more convincing from the text of the Phenomenology itself. For now, however, if we are to explain its purpose, we must examine what follows from the third and final feature of the philosophical knowledge that Phenomenology is meant to prepare. We must ask, in other words, what follows from its power to convince.

Only Phenomenology can, strictly speaking, give a complete answer to the question: “What is philosophy?” The nature of philosophy will become fully clear only at the end of Phenomenology, on the basis of its development as a whole. Only then will it become fully clear what the specifically philosophical “power to convince” must consist in.
To clarify the issue, we need to distinguish “opinion” from “knowledge,” and “ideology” from “truth.”

An “opinion” can happen to be correct. Its meaning may correspond to something that exists independently of it. But simply as an opinion, it can never guarantee that it is correct. Nothing therefore prevents us from accepting another opinion that differs fundamentally from the first or even directly contradicts it. Opinion, as such, is not “convincing” at all.

“Knowledge,” by contrast, is not contingent but necessary. To understand its meaning is at the same time to understand that this meaning is true and that its opposite is false. It is therefore precisely as knowledge that knowledge is “convincing.” And it is not convincing merely “today” or merely “for me.” It is convincing always and for everyone—at least for everyone who understands it.

“Ideology,” meanwhile, is true only in appearance, and appears true only to those whose interests it serves. “Truth,” by contrast, does not depend on particular “interests”—or, if one prefers, it corresponds to the permanent interests of everyone.

We can also say that an “ideology” correctly reflects not the reality expressed by its explicit meaning, but the conditions that produced that meaning—namely, “class interests.” “Truth,” by contrast, is nothing other than the disclosure, through meaning, of the reality that meaning expresses.
Phenomenology must therefore show the philosopher that genuine knowledge, properly understood, is possible.
First of all, it must expose the inadequacy of both the rationalist and the empiricist accounts of knowledge.
first, that mere “consistency”—the absence of internal contradiction—is not enough to make something genuinely convincing;

second, that if we examine only the consistency of different forms of discourse, we have no way to determine which is true and which is false. This also means that there are no so-called “self-evident truths” or “axioms requiring no proof”;
third, that the content of any discourse must, as a rule, originate in something that exists outside and independently of that discourse.

But the dialectic that accepts this final point from empiricism also reveals the inadequacy of empiricism itself. It shows that knowledge cannot be made convincing simply by comparing, within knowledge itself and using knowledge alone, the meaning of what we say with the reality that this meaning is supposed to express.

The dialectic of empiricism therefore leads onward to “experimentalism.” Experimentalism understands that knowledge can acquire convincing force only through practical verification: knowledge of nature must be tested “technically,” through work, while knowledge of the human world must be tested “revolutionarily,” through struggle.

Yet the internal dialectic of “experimentalism” shows that only perfect “knowledge”—that is, omniscience—can be definitively convincing. Technical and revolutionary verification can ultimately apply only to knowledge of a concrete being, and a concrete being cannot be separated from reality as a whole.
So, in the end, showing that “convincing” knowledge is possible means showing that omniscience is possible—that perfect knowledge, knowledge that can no longer change, or “wisdom,” can be reached.
And it is the entire content of Phenomenology—the complete dialectic it describes—that reveals this possibility.

By explaining the origin, or “genesis,” of human knowledge and the regular pattern of its development—its “evolution” or “progress”—Phenomenology shows that the idea of completed knowledge is not utopian. In other words, it shows that this development can reach the absolute limits of knowledge—or, more precisely, that it can exhaust all the discursive or “logical” possibilities of knowledge. This is not a fiction.
On the contrary, it is precisely Phenomenology’s description of the past and present development of knowledge that allows us to discover its future possibilities.
But to show that knowledge can continue to develop is also to show that present knowledge remains imperfect.

Phenomenology therefore does more than reveal to the philosopher that perfect knowledge is possible. It also shows how imperfect the knowledge available at the time of Phenomenology still is—an imperfection revealed by the fact that this knowledge is not yet fully convincing.
But showing this is not enough if knowledge is to be completed in a “real” rather than merely “utopian” way.

Phenomenology must not merely show the philosopher the “abstract” possibility of perfect knowledge. It must also reveal the real conditions under which existing knowledge can be brought closer to perfection.

It does this by showing where new historical conditions have emerged: new social, political, and technical conditions that did not exist when the knowledge we already possess was first produced. By understanding these new conditions, the philosopher gains the possibility of improving that knowledge.
